question: A RAG pipeline caches its retrieved documentation block using an ephemeral cache breakpoint placed after the documentation and before the user's question. Over the course of a week, several changes occur to the production system. Which of these events would invalidate the existing cache for that documentation block? (Select all that apply.)
options: A) A user submits a new, previously unseen follow-up question while the cached documentation stays identical.
B) The tool definitions available to the agent are modified.
C) The system instructions that precede the cached documentation block are edited.
D) The cache TTL configuration is changed from the default ephemeral setting to a 1-hour TTL.
E) The underlying retrieved document content is updated after a new retrieval run.
correct_answers: B) The tool definitions available to the agent are modified.
C) The system instructions that precede the cached documentation block are edited.
E) The underlying retrieved document content is updated after a new retrieval run.
explanations: Incorrect. The cache remains valid when only the user's query changes and the document content stays identical; this is precisely the case caching is designed to optimize, not invalidate.
Correct. Changing tool definitions is a documented cache-invalidating event, since tool definitions are part of what determines the cached prefix.
Correct. Modifying the system instructions that precede the cached block changes the content of that stable prefix, invalidating the existing cache entry.
Incorrect. Changing the TTL setting affects how long a future cache entry will persist; it is a configuration change for subsequent writes, not an event that invalidates the current cached content.
Correct. When retrieved documents are updated, the cached prefix no longer matches the new content, so the cache is invalidated and a new cache write occurs.
